snippet.title: A Detailed Look at the Black Death | 3 Hour History | Human Voiced, No Ads
snippet.description:
00:00:00 A General Plague History
00:51:28 How People Prepared for the Plague
01:33:15 Eyewitness Accounts of the Black Death
02:18:33 The Plague Returns! (To London)


Embark on a three-hour deep dive into one of the most devastating pandemics in human history: the Black Death. This exploration provides a comprehensive look at the plague from its origins to its resurgence during the Great Plague of London, enriched with eyewitness accounts and historical analysis to offer a vivid portrayal of its impact on society.

General History of the Black Death The journey begins with an overview of the Black Death, which ravaged Europe, Asia, and Africa in the mid-14th century, peaking in Europe from 1347 to 1351. Understand the origins of the plague, believed to have started in Asia and spread through trade routes, including the Silk Road, ultimately reaching the Crimea and Mediterranean ports. Explore the bacterium Yersinia pestis, transmitted by fleas hosted by rats, and how it caused bubonic, pneumonic, and septicemic forms of plague. The segment discusses the massive demographic shock and societal upheaval caused by the plague, which killed an estimated 75 to 200 million people, drastically reducing the world's population at that time.

Eyewitness Accounts Transition to a series of poignant eyewitness accounts from various regions, which paint a harrowing picture of the daily realities during the plague years. These narratives include writings from Giovanni Boccaccio in Italy, who described the societal breakdown in Florence. These firsthand accounts offer insights into the fear, mourning, and sometimes bizarre remedies that people resorted to in the face of the relentless pandemic.

The Great Plague of London Conclude with an examination of the Great Plague of London in 1665-1666, one of the last major outbreaks of the bubonic plague in England. Look into how the plague reached London, its symptoms, spread, and the social and economic ramifications for one of Europe's largest cities. Discuss the measures taken to control the disease, such as quarantine of the sick, the shutting down of public places, and the marking of plague houses with a red cross. Detail Samuel Pepys’ diaries, which provide a vivid, personal insight into life during the plague year in London. The segment also addresses the aftermath and changes in public health policies that arose from the crisis.


This three-hour narrative not only chronicles the tragic consequences of the Black Death but also celebrates human resilience and ingenuity in the face of such a catastrophic event. It provides a deep, educational, and engaging look at one of the pivotal points in human history, drawing lessons that resonate even in today's global health landscape.

Information sourced from Wiki, Gutenburg, JSTOR, primary and secondary sources. All information is congruent with archaeological and history evidence at the time of recording.

snippet.title: How The Bubonic Plague Killed 100,000 Londoners | The Great Plague | Absolute History
snippet.description:
The Great Plague of 1665 killed 100,000 Londoners - one in three of the people living in the city. While kept diaries have provided terrifying testaments to the horrors of that summer, other stories have been hidden in the archives of London churches for centuries. Rare documents unearthed in some of the cities oldest places of worship now tell the story of what it was like for an ordinary person, more often than not living in poverty, as the plague swept through London. This factual drama follows the lives of those living in Cock and Key Alley, one of the dank and dismal yards squeezed between Fleet Street and the Thames - and brings to life 17th Century London at one of its most frightening moments.

snippet.title: What Life Was Like During The Black Plague
snippet.description:
The Black Death remains one of the most significant pandemics in human history — a crisis that not only caused immense loss of life but also changed the course of Europe forever. Spreading between 1347 and 1352, the plague is believed to have taken the lives of tens of millions. Yet its legacy goes far beyond the numbers.

Originating in Central Asia and arriving in Europe through busy trade routes, the disease moved swiftly, touching major cities like Paris, Florence, and London. As it spread, communities were deeply affected — with towns falling quiet and daily life upended.

The aftermath of the Black Death led to major shifts in European society. Long-standing systems like feudalism began to weaken, and new opportunities emerged for workers. It also left a lasting mark on religion, medicine, and the arts, as people grappled with questions about life, loss, and meaning.

Join us as we uncover how a single event reshaped a continent and left a legacy still felt today.

The Great Plague of London caused widespread devastation. The streets were filled with carcasses waiting for burial and the agonizing cries of the dying echoed in the streets.
The plague spared no one, affecting people of all ages, classes, and genders, leading to a high mortality rate. The unsanitary conditions in 17th-century London, with open sewers, rampant rats, and contaminated water sources, contributed to the rapid spread of the plague. The impact of the plague was documented in weekly bills of mortality, listing the number and manner of deaths, while the dead were often collected in open carts and buried in mass plague pits.

snippet.title: 7 Days Surviving the Black Death in Medieval London | 1348 Full Documentary
snippet.description:
7 Days Surviving the Black Death in Medieval London — the complete series in one full-length documentary.

In the autumn of 1348, the Black Death arrived in London. Within months it would kill between a third and a half of everyone in the city. This is the story of that catastrophe — not told through kings, battles, or cathedrals, but through seven ordinary people living one day at a time as the plague closed in around them.

Over roughly an hour and a half, you'll spend a full week inside medieval London in 1348: walking the cobbled streets of Cheapside, standing in the cold choir stalls of Westminster Abbey, sitting in a physician's candlelit workroom, and watching the long burial trenches grow at East Smithfield. This is immersive, historically grounded living-history — a reconstruction of what daily life, work, faith, medicine, and death actually looked like for medieval Londoners during the worst pandemic in European history.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
📜 WHAT YOU'LL SEE — THE FULL WEEK
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
Day 1 — The Apprentice: a young weaver on Cheapside, watching the first death-carts roll past his master's workshop.
Day 2 —  The Monk
Day 3 — The Silk Woman: a craftswoman of Soper Lane fighting to keep her workshop and her trade alive as her workers fall ill.
Day 4 — The Gravedigger: a man at the East Smithfield burial ground who has stopped counting how many he has laid in the rows.
Day 5 — The Alderman: a ward official who keeps showing up to a half-empty Guildhall, quietly bending the rules to protect the living.
Day 6 — The Physician: a Montpellier-trained doctor with the wrong theory, the right instincts, and a notebook filling with the names of the dead.
Day 7 — The Survivor: the whole city, six weeks in — what London lost, what it kept, and why it is still here almost seven centuries later.


━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
🏰 ABOUT THIS SERIES
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
This is the complete "A Week in Medieval London (1348)" series from Time Warp Cities — a channel that reconstructs the daily texture of the past, one day, one life, and one city at a time. If you're fascinated by the Black Death, the bubonic plague, the Middle Ages, medieval England, and the real social history of how ordinary people lived, worked, and died, this full documentary is made for you.

We cover the history of the plague in London: how it spread along trade routes from Europe, why medieval medicine and miasma theory failed against it, what the East Smithfield mass burials reveal to archaeologists today, how the labour shortage that followed cracked the foundations of feudalism, and how the city survived and rebuilt — through 1348, the later plague returns, the Great Fire of 1666, and beyond.

snippet.title: Ancient DNA Finally Reveals the REAL Origin of the Black Death
snippet.description:
Where did the Black Death—the deadliest pandemic in recorded history—truly begin?

For centuries, its origins were shrouded in mystery. But a forgotten cemetery near Lake Issyk Kul in Kyrgyzstan has revealed stunning new evidence. In this documentary-style deep dive, we explore how 800-year-old graves, ancient inscriptions, and cutting-edge DNA analysis led scientists to pinpoint the true birthplace of the plague that killed tens of millions across Europe, Asia, and North Africa.

Learn how a single strain of Yersinia pestis, preserved in the teeth of medieval plague victims, was identified as the ancestral source of the Black Death. Discover how trade routes, climate change, and human mobility allowed a microscopic killer to reshape global history—and how modern science finally uncovered the origin of it all.

Based on groundbreaking research published in Science, this is the story of how the past continues to speak through stone, bone, and DNA.

Source:
Gibbons, Ann. 800-year-old graves pinpoint where the Black Death began, Science.

snippet.title: The Black Death Killed 60% Of Medieval Europe's Population
snippet.description:
The Black Death and the 14th Century's greatest catastrophe explored with Dr. Helen Carr. In this episode, Dan Snow dives into the "Calamitous 14th Century," a period defined by the Great Famine, ceaseless deluges, and the arrival of Yersinia pestis. We trace the plague’s journey from the Mongol Empire and the Silk Roads to the port cities of Italy and the shores of Dorset, revealing how a biological phenomenon intersected with medieval politics and military sieges to wipe out nearly 60% of Europe's population.

From the rise of the "Momento Mori" cult and the Flagellants to the economic empowerment of the peasant class and the "Golden Age" for women, we examine how the survivors rebuilt a fractured world. Discover the grisly reality of bubos, the origins of quarantine, and the lasting legacy of the Black Death on the modern Western world.

snippet.title: ⚡ The Black Death — The Untold Story | Documentary Film
snippet.description:
⚡ In the autumn of 1347, twelve ships sailed into a Sicilian harbor — and no one on shore could have known they were about to witness the end of the medieval world.
The Black Death killed somewhere between a third and half of all Europeans in just six years. You know the horror. You know the numbers. But here's what most history classes never tell you: the worst pandemic in human history didn't just destroy the medieval world — it accidentally, brutally, against everyone's will, built the modern one. Discover how a bacterium traveling on a flea's back shattered the feudal system, cracked the authority of the Church, created the first labor market in European history, and planted the seeds of the Renaissance, the Reformation, and the individual rights you live inside of today.
Follow this story from the rodent colonies of Central Asia to a Mongol siege weapon made of corpses, from the rotting streets of Florence to the first moment a peasant could look his lord in the eye and say no.

snippet.title: The Black Death: Europe's Greatest Catastrophe - Complete History | 3 Hour Deep Dive
snippet.description:
In 1347, a disease arrived in Europe that would kill half the continent in five years. The Black Death wasn't just a pandemic—it was the catastrophe that ended the medieval world and created the foundations of modern Europe.

This is the complete story. Three hours examining every aspect: how it arrived, how it spread, how medieval people responded, how society collapsed and rebuilt, and what lessons this greatest of catastrophes holds for understanding human civilization.

🕰️ TIMESTAMPS:

00:23:37 - Part Two: The Arrival (From Caffa to Sicily, 1346-1347)
00:41:26 - Part Three: The Spread (How Plague Consumed a Continent)
01:06:38 - Part Four: Medical Responses (Plague Doctors & Medieval Medicine)
01:24:00 - Part Five: Human Darkness (Scapegoating & Social Breakdown)
01:38:41 - Part Six: The Last Day of a Village (Wharram Percy's Story)
01:56:23 - Part Seven: Society Collapses (The End of Feudalism)

02:49:46 - Part Ten: Lessons from the Abyss (What the Black Death Teaches)

The bubonic plague, which killed around 1/5 of the world’s population in the 14th century, is still around today -- but it now claims only a few thousand lives each year. How did that number shrink so drastically? Sharon N. DeWitte investigates the causes and effects of the black death and explains how knowing this information can help us prepare for any future outbreaks of the disease.

snippet.title: How You Could Have Survived the Black Plague
snippet.description:
The Black Death is a plague that changed the world. As the most profound epidemic in human history, the plague claimed the lives of millions, with nearly half of Europe's population perishing from the disease. Some feared they were living through the apocalypse amidst the chaotic upheaval, while others turned to sinful pleasure during the plague to distract from the horror. And as for what happened to victims of the plague, well, it wasn't opportune.

Surviving the Black Death wasn't easy. How did someone protect themselves from it and who did they blame when they got sick? What happened to their body as the infection spread? The only certainty was demise; after all, bubonic plague in the Middle Ages didn't spare anyone: monks and nuns perished alongside mothers and their children, rich men, and even royalty. 

Here's how plague victims lived day-to-day.

The disease known as the plague has been stalking humanity for over 5,000 years, and there have been many outbreaks. In fact, there have been three pandemics caused by the bacillus bacterium Yersinia Pestis. The first was in the 6th century. It devastated the Byzantine Empire and was known as The Plague of Justinian. The third began in China in the mid-19th century and quickly spread throughout the world. But it is the plague that began in 1346 which killed more than 50 million people in just seven years that we refer to as the ‘Black Death’. The Middle Ages was a time of superstition, religious fanaticism and ignorance and so they thought it was the end of the world. In reality it was the largest pandemic in the history of humanity.
